objects: conditional meta-analysis; pooled genotypes; stepwise SNP selection
assumptions: many participating studies; pooled individual-level genotypes unavailable
conclusion: Repeated study-level conditional meta-analysis is administratively onerous and makes stepwise SNP selection impractical.
scope: Motivation for a summary-data conditional analysis.
span: For meta-analysis of a large number of participating studies, however, pooled individual-level genotype data are usually unavailable, such that conditional analysis can only be performed at the level of individual studies. Summary results from individual studies are then collected and combined through a second round of meta-analysis. This procedure is administratively onerous.

conclusion: Quantitative phenotypes are modeled by the additive multi-SNP linear model y = Xb + e, with centered genotype coding and joint SNP effects b.
scope: Linear regression model; this passage does not impose a Gaussian residual distribution.

objects: selected SNP set; conditional P values; optimized joint model
conclusion: Genome-wide stepwise selection adds SNPs according to conditional P values and estimates joint effects after model optimization.
scope: Fixed-effect stepwise model selection; no effect prior or penalty is specified in this definition.
span: We adopt a genome-wide stepwise selection procedure to select SNPs on the basis of conditional P values and estimate the joint effects of all selected SNPs after the model has been optimized.

objects: P-value inclusion cutoff; squared multiple-correlation cutoff
conclusion: The stepwise procedure uses a P-value cutoff for model initiation and a squared multiple-correlation cutoff to screen collinear SNPs.
scope: Tunable thresholds, illustrated by 5E-8 and 0.9; these are not population assumptions.
span: Start with a model with the most significant SNP in the single-SNP meta-analysis across the whole genome with P value below a cutoff P value, such as 5 × 10–8.For the tth step, calculate the P values of all the remaining SNPs conditional on the SNP(s) that have already been selected in the model. To avoid problems due to colinearity, if the squared multiple correlation between a SNP to be tested and the selected SNP(s) is larger than a cutoff value, such as 0.9, the conditional P value for that SNP will be set to 1.

objects: selected SNP effects; number of SNPs; inclusion threshold
assumptions: fixed-effect model selection; number of SNPs much larger than sample size
conclusion: Stepwise fixed-effect selection risks overfitting and winner's-curse effect inflation, with false-positive inclusion at less stringent thresholds.
scope: Selection bias warning; no unbiasedness guarantee for selected effects.
span: As with any fixed-effect model selection strategy, such as stepwise linear multiple regression analysis, there is a risk of over-fitting effects. This can be a particular problem for the analysis of GWAS SNP data because the number of SNPs is typically much larger than the experimental sample size. The effects of selected SNPs tend to be overestimated (sometimes called the winner's curse) and, if the threshold for inclusion is less stringent, false positives could be included in the model.

objects: residual variance; phenotypic variance; conditional and joint test error rates
assumptions: residual variance held constant at phenotypic variance during SNP selection
conclusion: The authors state that fixing residual variance at phenotypic variance keeps false-positive rates at the meta-analysis level, while potentially losing power.
scope: Author-stated calibration claim for the conservative procedure; not a finite-sample theorem for arbitrary reference LD error.
span: In practice, we keep the residual variance constant to the phenotypic variance, even if we added significant SNPs into the model, which may be too conservative and may therefore result in a loss of power to detect additional associated variants but has the benefit of keeping the false positive rate in the conditional and joint analysis at the same level as in the meta-analysis.

objects: summary-data joint analysis; full discovery genotype reference
assumptions: single GWAS cohort; whole discovery sample used as reference
conclusion: When the full discovery cohort supplies the reference genotypes, the method becomes equivalent to multiple regression analysis.
scope: Equivalence is conditional on using the whole discovery sample as reference.
span: Our method is not limited to meta-analysis summary data but can also be applied to a single GWAS cohort with individual-level genotypes, in which case, the whole discovery sample is used as the reference sample, and our method then becomes equivalent to a multiple regression analysis (Online Methods and Supplementary Fig. 6).

objects: summary-level association statistics; reference LD corrections
assumptions: meta-analysis summary statistics and a reference sample
conclusion: The authors describe their summary-data LD-correction approach as similar to the approach of Sonesson, Meuwissen and Goddard (2010).
scope: Similarity is stated; the paper does not assert full equivalence to the cited aquaculture genomic-selection method.
span: We propose an approximate conditional and joint analysis approach using summary-level statistics from a meta-analysis and LD corrections between SNPs estimated from a reference sample, such as a subset of the meta-analysis sample, using an approach similar to one previously described12.

objects: genomic control; population stratification; polygenic genomic inflation
assumptions: absence of population stratification; polygenic inheritance
conclusion: The authors argue that double genomic-control correction may be overly conservative because polygenic inheritance can itself cause genomic inflation.
scope: Conditional rationale for omitting the second correction; not a general guarantee that stratification is absent.
span: First, the purpose of genomic control correction is to adjust for the effect of population stratification, but, in the absence of population stratification and presence of polygenic inheritance, genomic inflation is expected21; therefore, double-GC correction might be too conservative and overkill.

objects: disease liabilities L; logistic residuals; joint and marginal log odds ratios
assumptions: liability model L = Xb + e; effect sizes and standard errors on the log(OR) scale
conclusion: The authors extend the quantitative-trait calculations to case-control analysis on the log-odds-ratio scale, stating that least-squares effect estimates remain unbiased with logistic residuals.
scope: Author-stated liability-model extension; not an assertion of equality between linear and logistic maximum-likelihood fits.
span: Even though the residuals follow a logistic distribution, the least-squares estimates of effect sizes are unbiased, because the least-squares approach does not rely on the assumption of normality. Hence, we can apply the same methods as described above for a quantitative trait to a case-control study, as long as the effect sizes and standard errors are expressed on the log(OR) scale.
